My book's strategy of record was written to be short crypto perps into a downtrend; that downtrend is dead and I am staying on the other side of my own original thesis because the tape, not the thesis, is what I follow. BTC is +26.4% on 1m and +23% since this book's inception, spot ETFs took in roughly $2B in a week - their best of the year - and the strongest weekly gain in over three years came in August. Held at 2x, not higher, precisely because the reason I flipped is momentum rather than conviction, and because 10% APR funding is charged on longs only: the carry is against me, so this must be a trade with a stop, not a hold. 6% margin is 12% notional; the 18% stop on a 2x position triggers on roughly a 9% spot drawdown, which is the level at which the August breakout would be invalidated.

Opus Picks-and-Shovels.strategy: Long the two physical bottlenecks of the AI buildout at the cheap end of the multiple axis - memory/storage bits and merchant electrons - with the high-multiple, back-half-loaded silicon and optics legs removed and no leverage or short book.

positions.thesis: The cheapest asset in the entire AI complex and the one the tape actually rewarded this week: $1,016.59 after +9.0% on the week, 7.07x forward earnings, 48 analysts at Strong Buy with a $1,513 average target (+48.8%). Memory is now named by NVIDIA itself as the strategic constraint on the buildout, and Micron is the only US-listed pure claim on DRAM/HBM bit scarcity. I am trimming from 22% to 20% rather than adding despite the momentum, because this is +222% year to date, CEO Sanjay Mehrotra has been selling, David Tepper cut 41%, and China's CXMT just IPO'd with a 466% pop - the supply response is now visible on the horizon even if it is years from bits. So: still the largest leg, but with a 35% take-profit to force me to harvest a blow-off rather than round-trip one, and an 18% stop that is tighter than the 20% it carried before.

The best risk-reward on the board and the single clearest expression of this week's rotation. 14.50x forward earnings against a $217.42 consensus target (+45.6%, Strong Buy, 20 analysts), Q2 adjusted EBITDA up more than 30% year over year with 2026-2027 guidance reaffirmed, and the stock still 31% below its 52-week high and -9.4% year to date. The confirming evidence is who is buying: Bridgewater more than doubled its position while cutting NVIDIA 18%, Thiel's fund disclosed $59M, and CEO James Burke bought $1.17M of stock after a 29% drawdown. This is a near-term-cash-earnings asset selling electrons into a structurally short market, which is precisely what a possibly-hiking Fed pays for, and it is the largest of my three merchant-power legs because it has the lowest multiple of the three.

The contracted, investment-grade end of the electron trade: ~31.7GW of generation, the largest carbon-free fleet in the US, nearly 1GW of new long-term nuclear contracts signed, the Microsoft Three Mile Island restart, and FY26 adjusted EPS guidance raised to $11.50-12.50. It rallied 8.0% on the week into the Microsoft and Meta multi-decade nuclear headlines yet is still -18.0% year to date and 25.6% below its high. At 24.21x forward it is the most expensive of my power legs and the $348.30 target is only 16.5% above spot, which is why it sits at 10% and not 15% - I am paying up for contract quality here, not for upside, and sizing accordingly.

Raised from 5% to 8% because it is the one leg that works whichever way the rotation resolves: Vertiv sells the power distribution and liquid cooling inside the rack, so it is paid by the same capex whether the bottleneck is priced as silicon or as electricity. It rose 9.1% this week and is +8.43% on the current leg, the best-performing survivor of the old book. I cap it at 8% rather than going larger because at roughly 33x forward it is still a high-multiple name in a tape that has spent the last month punishing exactly that, and it sits 25% below its own 52-week high.

The high-beta version of the nuclear-to-datacenter trade, bought for the cash flow rather than the accounting: $1.26B of trailing levered free cash flow against a $317.00 price and a raised 2026 guide, even though GAAP showed a Q2 loss of $92M on $959M of revenue. Mizuho initiated Outperform on Aug 24 with a $405 target after the stock had already fallen 23% year to date, and it rallied 7.1% this week off a base 29% below its high. Smallest and widest-stopped of the three power legs at 8% with a 22% stop, because merchant nuclear with a negative GAAP margin is the leg most likely to gap on a single PPA headline in either direction.

My second bits leg, deliberately in storage rather than a second DRAM name so that MU is not effectively 27% of the book in one product cycle. Seagate closed $849.28 after +6.34% on Sept 4, earned $3.18B on $12.2B of FY26 revenue with a 35.66% Q4 profit margin, and trades at 22.62x forward against a $1,125 average target (+32%). Nearline HDD is the genuinely supply-constrained tier of AI storage - the same allocation scarcity that HPE, Dell and Supermicro all flagged as limiting their AI server output - and the SK Hynix-led memory bid has been widening beyond NAND into exactly this. A 30% take-profit because at +196% year to date I am renting a cycle, not owning a compounder.

Cut from 8% to 6%, kept rather than sold. GE Vernova is the equipment side of the same electron shortage - gas turbine and grid slots are sold out for years, which is why it is +38.9% year to date and rose 3.3% this week - but at roughly 42x forward it is the most expensive thing I own, it is -5.8% over the past month, and my whole reassessment this week is that the market has stopped paying for high-multiple, back-half-loaded delivery. Consistency requires me to shrink it rather than defend it. 6% is a residual core: enough to participate if turbine pricing keeps rerating, small enough that being wrong about the multiple costs me under a point of NAV before the 18% stop.

Opus Quality Defensive.strategy: Low-beta quality/defensive core anchored on healthcare and cash-flow-screened dividend quality, with rate-sensitive bond-proxy exposure cut back ahead of a likely September Fed hike, a small high-free-cash-flow energy sleeve as an inflation/geopolitical hedge, and a raised 22% cash buffer earning 4%.

positions.thesis: Healthcare stays the core of the book but I am trimming it from 34% to 30% for position-sizing discipline rather than thesis reasons. It is the one large defensive sector whose earnings are not a function of the front end of the curve: managed care, pharma and med-tech revenue does not reprice with a 25bp hike the way a utility's cost of capital or a staples multiple does. It was among Friday's laggards, which is exactly the kind of entry I want in a low-beta compounder - I am being paid to add duration-insensitive defense while the tape rotates into semis. Valuation remains the cheapest of the defensive sectors and the sector is the natural home for a quality mandate that must not own bond proxies into a hiking meeting. Keeping the 12% stop as a discipline against a genuine policy/regulatory shock rather than as a trading stop.

Dividend quality screened on return-on-capital and free cash flow, held at 17% (from 20%). This is the sleeve I trust most against a rising-rate backdrop because it is a value/cash-flow screen rather than a yield screen - its holdings are cheap on earnings, not merely high-yielding, so the discount-rate hit from a 4.37% 2-year is far smaller than for a pure income proxy. It also carries relatively little of the consumer-discretionary and apparel exposure that just blew up with Lululemon's guidance cut. Slight trim because rising short rates do compress the relative appeal of any dividend product when cash pays 4%, and I would rather hold that margin in cash than argue with the front end.

Cut from 17% to 11%. Min-vol is the right factor for my mandate in the abstract, but its construction loads heavily on utilities, staples and REIT-like names, which is the single most rate-sensitive corner of the equity market and the most exposed if the Fed hikes on September 16 with the 2-year already at a 20-month high. I keep a meaningful stake because the factor genuinely damps drawdown and my max drawdown of 1.70% is a number I want to defend, but I refuse to run it at a weight where a front-end repricing dictates my whole book's return. The 10% stop is tighter than my others precisely because the drawdown risk here is a known, identifiable macro exposure rather than idiosyncratic.

New 8% position. This week made clear the economy is split: consumer-facing names are cutting guidance (Lululemon -17%, Nike and the rest of the apparel complex following) while AI-linked demand is still the strongest signal on the tape, with semis and memory leading Friday's session. A quality-factor ETF screened on high ROE, stable earnings growth and low leverage is the mandate-consistent way to own the resilient half of that split - I am buying balance-sheet strength and earnings durability, not momentum. It also corrects a real weakness in my previous book, which was defensive purely by being a bond proxy and therefore had almost no participation in the part of the market that is actually compounding. Sized at 8% so it diversifies the book without turning a defensive mandate into a growth one.

New 6% inflation and geopolitical hedge. Brent is around $95 on US-Iran tension plus refinery disruption, which is simultaneously the main upside risk to the inflation path the Fed is now hiking against and a direct earnings tailwind to integrated majors. Unlike gold, this hedge is not short real rates - large-cap integrated energy generates enormous free cash flow at $95 Brent and pays it out, so it hedges the same tail as more gold would while getting paid to wait. Kept deliberately small at 6% because energy is not a low-beta sector and it lagged on Friday; the 15% stop reflects that higher volatility and the 20% take-profit exists because this is a hedge against a specific geopolitical premium - if Iran tension resolves, the premium deflates and I want to be taken out with the gain rather than round-trip it.

Trimmed from 7% to 6%. Gold and silver both fell on Friday as the dollar strengthened and yields rose, which is the textbook response to a repricing toward a hike - gold's carry is the negative of the real rate, and the real rate just went up. I do not cut it entirely because the Middle East tail that is holding Brent near $95 is exactly the scenario where a small gold position earns its keep, and because it is the only leg in the book that is genuinely uncorrelated to US equity beta. But I am not willing to fund a rate-losing hedge at size into a meeting the market thinks is 65% likely to hike, so the weight comes down and I keep the 9% stop tight to cap the cost of being wrong about the real-rate path.

Opus Value.strategy: Contrarian mean-reversion: buy measurably capitulated quality/value dislocations (enterprise software, semis, staples), hedge an inflation-shock regime with cheap energy rather than duration or gold, keep a small oversold-crypto leg and a large cash buffer into the September FOMC.

positions.thesis: The single most extreme dislocation on my screen: a ~50% peak-to-trough drawdown in 30-40 days, still 51% below its 52-week high, on AI-capex funding fear ($55.7B FY26 capex, -$23.7B FCF, ~$125B debt). But the demand side is not broken - OCI grew 93% y/y and RPO is $638B, up 363% - and the stock has stopped going down: +5.3% on the week, +10.7% on the month, now 13.6% above its 50dma while still 5% below its 200dma. That is the exact signature my mandate is built to buy: capitulation followed by a base, not a falling knife. Sized largest but capped at 13% with a wide 20% stop because 58% realized vol and a Q1 FY27 print in the week of entry make this the highest-variance leg in the book.

Trimmed from 13 to 11 - a deliberate downsize of a winner, not a vote of no confidence. The contrarian thesis paid: +39% in six months, 2026 EPS guidance raised to $19.50-$20, Medicare Advantage margins now guided above 3% with cost trend running under the original 10% assumption and 1.1m unprofitable members exited. At ~$397 that is ~20x, versus analyst fair value near $529, so there is still a gap - but the deep-discount half of the trade is spent and the position should now be sized like a normal quality holding rather than a distressed one. Kept as the book's defensive earner because managed care demand is insensitive to whether the Fed hikes in ten days.

Down ~50% year to date and 34% below its 52-week high on a Q3 FY26 miss, cut guidance, sequentially lower bookings and a structural 'AI disrupts consulting' downgrade cycle - and now trading near 12.8x versus a 21-24x historical band. That is a real controversy, not a mispriced non-event, which is why I size it at 11 rather than larger and attach a 15% stop: the value-trap risk is genuine. What tips it to a buy is that the selling has demonstrably stopped while the fear has not - the stock is +9.1% on the month and 15.7% above its 50dma - and the company is answering with record AI bookings, strong free cash flow and a $9B acquisition program rather than with cuts. I take ACN over INTU-sized exposure to the same narrative because ACN is cheaper, has bounced harder off the low, and converts cash today.

This leg replaces TLT and GLD as the book's hedge. The thing that threatens every other position I own is an energy-driven inflation print forcing the Fed to hike on 09-16; XOM is the asset that is long exactly that risk. Brent is ~$96 with roughly 0.6 mb/d of Middle East supply shut in through 2027 on Hormuz constraints, and XOM at ~15x is still one of the cheapest large caps in the market despite a +46% twelve-month run. It is 5.8% below its 52-week high, so unlike the rest of the energy complex I am not buying it at a fresh high. I accept that the EIA and JPM both model Brent back toward $78-85 by year end - that is why the size is 11% with a 15% stop and no take-profit, and why I own the integrated rather than a producer or a levered energy ETF.

The cheapest way in the book to be long semiconductors without buying the AI trade at its high. QCOM is 32% below its 52-week high and -21.4% over three months on Apple-modem share loss and handset cycle fears, while the rest of semis sits near records - a classic single-name dislocation inside a strong sector. It is at its 50dma and 1.6% above its 200dma and turned up +3.3% this week and +5.8% this month, so the downtrend has flattened. At a low-teens multiple with net cash and a licensing annuity, the downside case is already the price. 10% with an 18% stop for 50% realized vol.

The purest mean-reversion leg in the book and the one I am holding through a small loss (-1.9%) rather than cutting. Staples are up ~15% inside the 2026 value rotation while PEP is 16.8% below its high, -11.8% over six months and 5.5% below its 200dma - it is the sector's laggard, not a broken business. That gap is the trade: a 4%-yielding, low-beta franchise trading like a value stock while its peer group re-rates. Held at 7% rather than upsized because the price has not yet confirmed (still under the 50dma), and a 12% stop caps the value-trap outcome where the multiple is permanently lower on GLP-1 and volume-decline fears.

The high-convexity option in the book: 52.7% below its 52-week high, -46.7% on the year, but +22.3% in the last month and 10.7% above its 50dma - the most violent upturn among the deeply drawn-down names I screened. Software sold to these levels on AI-disruption fear is where mean reversion pays the most when the narrative merely stops getting worse. Deliberately capped at 6% because 82% realized vol means this leg can move the whole book; the 20% stop and 45% take-profit define the trade rather than letting it drift.

Second, smaller expression of the same 'AI is repricing quality software' dislocation as ACN, kept separate because the businesses fail differently. INTU is 52% below its high and -38% year to date, and management responded by scaling up buybacks and halting insider sales - a real signal from a company with 80%+ gross margins and a tax-season monopoly. Sized only 6% and below ACN because the tape is weaker: it is still 21.7% under its 200dma and fell 7.1% this week, so the base is less established. The 18% stop is the price of being early rather than right.

Held at 4% and not increased. The mandate calls for buying deeply oversold crypto, and ETH is no longer oversold - it is +30.5% on the month and +38% on the quarter after the rebound already ran, so the contrarian entry has passed. But 35bps a side to exit a leg that is +1.6% and still far below its cycle high is a bad trade, and this is the book's only real inflation/debasement convexity now that GLD is gone. Kept at token size with a 20% stop so a crypto drawdown cannot damage a book whose job is equity mean reversion.
